title: 100-kyr climate cycles caused by 2.4-Myr eccentricity-modulated carbon cycles

paper_content.abstract: Earth’s climate has been dominated by ~100-kyr glacial cycles over the past ~800 ka, yet the mechanism remains debated. Here, we present correlation analyses of spectral power ratios of global records spanning the past 2.7 Ma, revealing a persistent anticorrelation between ~21-kyr and ~100-kyr power ratios, but no significant relationship between ~41-kyr and ~100-kyr power ratios. This suggests that ~100-kyr climate cycles are more related to eccentricity-modulated precession than to obliquity. Phase analyses of benthic δ18O/ice volume and δ13C (carbon cycle) since Antarctic glaciation onset (~34 Ma) show that strong ~100-kyr cycles emerged only when these proxies were phase-coupled. Such coupling recurred at ~2.4-Myr eccentricity maxima during the unipolar regime (before 7.5 Ma) and minima during the bipolar regime (after 4 Ma), explaining the persistent ~21-kyr/~100-kyr anticorrelation because eccentricity modulates precession amplitude. We propose that internal carbon cycle dynamics and ~2.4-Myr eccentricity-modulated δ¹⁸O/ice volume–δ¹³C coupling amplified ~100-kyr climate cycles not only over the past ~800 ka but since 34 Ma. Given that eccentricity will remain low for the next 400 kyr, ~100-kyr periodicities may continue to dominate future climate variability, assuming Earth remains in a bipolar regime.
paper_content.introduction:
As global cooling progressed through the Cenozoic, Arctic ice sheets began developing in the late Miocene, and large Northern Hemisphere ice sheets first emerged at the onset of the Pleistocene (~2.6-million-year age; Ma), marking Earth’s shift from a unipolar to a bipolar ice-sheet regime. Since then, Earth’s climate has been characterized by periodical glacial-interglacial cycles. The alignment of glacial cycles with astronomical periodicities leads to linking these climate cycles to variations in Earth’s orbital geometry and axial inclination that cause the insolation received on Earth to fluctuate at the frequency of obliquity (~1/41 kyr−1), precession (~1/19 and 1/23 kyr−1), and eccentricity (~1/100 and ~1/400 kyr−1). Obliquity alters the latitudinal distribution of insolation and seasonal contrast; precession affects the timing and intensity of seasons relative to Earth’s position in its elliptical orbit; and eccentricity influences the Earth–Sun distance, modulating the total insolation received by Earth. However, during the period after the Mid-Pleistocene Transition (MPT) (~800–1200 ka), the glacial-interglacial cycles display a dominant ~100-kyr cyclicities, no astronomical parameter could directly produce such strong ~100-kyr oscillations. This is because precession and obliquity cannot directly generate periodicities at ~100-kyr band, and eccentricity’s effect on total insolation is too weak to explain the strong ~100-kyr glacial power, despite eccentricity can produce ~100-kyr cycles. Amplitude mismatch between ~100 kyr cycles in eccentricity and climate, and the absence of the 405-kyr power in benthic foraminiferal oxygen isotope (δ18O), complicate the understanding of the ~100-kyr glacial cycles.

Before the MPT, glacial cycles were directly attributed to obliquity due to dominant ~40-kyr cyclicities, though interpretations for the dominance remain diverse. This idea was extended to explain the post-MPT ~100-kyr glacial cycles as a quantum of 2–3 obliquity cycles. Indeed, convincing evidence confirms obliquity’s role in late Pleistocene glacial terminations. However, the precession and obliquity phases of glacial terminations based on 230Th-dated speleothem chronology reveal that late Pleistocene glacial terminations have a closer relationship with precession than obliquity. This finding supports interpreting ~100-kyr cycles as a quantum of 4–6 precession cycles or a result of a beat between the main precessional frequencies. The research on the morphology of deglaciation/termination of glacial cycles further unveils that precession has more influence on deglacial onset, while obliquity is more important for attainment of peak interglacial conditions and glacial inception.

Despite these phase analyses confirm the role of astronomical forcing in driving glacial cycles, the mechanism behind dominant ~100-kyr power remains unclear. A comparison based on spectral analysis suggests that variations in inclination of Earth’s orbital plane could explain late Pleistocene ~100-kyr cycles. However, this is contested as an artifact of spectral methods, because unlike inclination’s singular ~100-kyr peak, glacial cycles exhibit variable ~80–120 kyr coeval periodicities.

In contrast to the external astronomical origin, late Pleistocene ~100-kyr glacial cycles were thought as the self-sustained oscillation driven by internal climate feedbacks. However, the solely internal mechanisms produce arbitrary phase, conflicting with the observed phase-locking between ~100-kyr cycles of eccentricity and climate. Thus, the plausible explanation for the late-Pleistocene ~100-kyr glacial cycle lies on the models that express these cycles as a nonlinear interaction between orbitally forced response (precession and obliquity) and the internal dynamics of atmosphere, oceans, ice sheets and lithosphere. This nonlinearity invokes a set of internal feedbacks to channel some of the system’s potential power into the ~100-kyr band. It is accepted that the ~100-kyr glacial cycles were phase-locked to eccentricity over the last 1.2 Ma, thus, the key to decoding the strong ~100-kyr glacial cycles depends on finding out the power source that amplifies the ~100-kyr spectral power. Both nonlinear response to precession and obliquity can produce ~100-kyr cycles, potentially amplifying ~100-kyr glacial power. Thus, confirming a potential link between the strong ~100-kyr glacial power and eccentricity-modulated precession or obliquity is pivotal to understanding glacial cycles. In this regard, analyzing the spectral power ratio relationship among the ~100-kyr cycles, precession, and obliquity components could provide clues.

The spectral power ratio relationship solely based on benthic δ18O lack statistical significance because the reverse relationship between the ~21-kyr and ~100-kyr power ratios in δ18O is masked by a nearly antiphase relationship between the ~41-kyr and ~100-kyr power ratio over the last 800 ka, which obscures the roles of precession and obliquity in amplifying ~100-kyr power. Nevertheless, as mentioned above, given that the ~100-kyr glacial cycles were closely related to internal processes, the 100-kyr cycles across climate components should be highly correlated with each other through a series of positive and negative feedbacks, despite potential time lags or leads between the forcing and the climate feedback. For example, the expansion and retreat of Pleistocene ice sheets could perturbate sea level and atmospheric-oceanic circulations via meltwater pulses and reshape Earth’s energy budget through albedo feedback. Consequently, the spectral power ratio relationship between precession/obliquity and the ~100-kyr components, preserved in ice volume or δ18O, should be projected onto other climate archives that are significantly affected by ice sheets. We therefore examine the spectral power ratio relationship among various paleoclimate proxies, including benthic δ18O, to explore the ~100-kyr glacial cycles. The spectral power ratio serves as a proxy for estimating spectral strength or variance within a specific frequency band (see Methods).

Given the shift from dominant ~40-kyr to ~100-kyr glacial cycles after the MPT and the current availability of high-resolution paleoclimate data, here, we statistically analyze spectral power ratio relationship among the ~21-kyr, ~41-kyr, and ~100-kyr components within datasets across 57 globally distributed paleoclimate archives (including ocean, loess, ice core, and other archives) from 33 sites. These continuous records span pre-MPT (1200–2700 ka), MPT (800–1200 ka), and post-MPT (0–800 ka) intervals, all with robust age models and a high temporal resolution of at least a 2-kyr sampling rate. The ~100-kyr power ratios display persistent negative correlation with ~21-kyr power ratios across these three intervals, while no relationship with ~41-kyr power ratios. Notably, strong/amplified ~100-kyr climate cycles also occurred before the Pleistocene, such as during the Pliocene, Miocene, and Oligocene. To test whether these earlier ~100-kyr climate cycles share a similar mechanism with those of the past 800 ka, we extend the analysis to the Eocene–Oligocene Transition (EOT; ~34 Ma), when the Antarctic ice sheet began to develop, by exploring the phase relationship between ice volume/benthic δ18O and benthic δ13C. It turns out that ~100-kyr climate cycles were periodically amplified, coinciding with δ18O/ice volume–δ13C phase coupling, which recurred at ~2.4-Myr eccentricity maxima (before 7.5 Ma) and minima (after 4 Ma).
paper_content.results:
The power decomposition analysis (PDA) (see Methods) was used to quantitatively estimate the spectral strength at frequencies corresponding to precession, obliquity, and ~100-kyr bands in paleoclimate records. Figure 2 presents the summarized PDA results for the collected 57 datasets, each based on their original age models, while detailed PDA results are shown in Figs. S2–S5. For comparisons, the overall power ratios of the ~100-kyr, ~41-kyr, and ~21-kyr cycles are shown using box whisker plots (Fig. 2A–C). To ensure significance, only PDA results with spectral power exceeding the 90% significance level at ~1/21 kyr−1, ~1/41 kyr−1, and ~1/100 kyr−1 were included. Detailed spectral estimations of these datasets are provided in Figs. S6–S9.

Post-MPT ~100-kyr power ratios exceed those of the pre-MPT interval in all datasets, while the opposite trend occurs for ~41-kyr power ratios. These shifts align with the transition from dominant ~41-kyr to ~100-kyr glacial cycles, confirming glacial influence on these records (Fig. 2A, C). Most paleoclimate records over the past ~800 ka show an inverse correlation between the ~100-kyr and ~21-kyr power ratios (Fig. 2A, B), a relationship that persists during and before the MPT (Fig. 2A, B). In contrast, the ~100-kyr power ratio shows no significant correlation with the ~41-kyr power ratio (Fig. 2A, C). Further analysis using the median power ratio values for the ~21-kyr, ~41-kyr, and ~100-kyr bands, represented by the horizontal lines in the box whisker plots, confirms a consistent negative correlation between the ~100-kyr and ~21-kyr power ratios (Fig. 2D, F, H), and no correlation between the ~100-kyr and ~41-kyr power ratios (Fig. 2E, G, I). Heterogeneity in dataset length, age models, and orbital tuning do not influence these relationship (Fig. S10C–F). Additionally, adjusting the frequency bandwidth setting in the PDA does not alter these relationships among the ~21-kyr, ~41-kyr, and ~100-kyr power ratios (Fig. S11).
paper_content.methods:
Extracting precession, obliquity and ~100-kyr spectral power ratios
To detect long-term evolution of changes in the spectral strength (or variance) of precession, obliquity, and ~100-kyr cycles in the collected climate archives, the evolutionary spectral power ratios at the precession, obliquity, and ~100-kyr bands to the total spectral power of the climate datasets were estimated. The estimation includes three steps. (1) Initially, the evolutionary power spectra of the datasets were calculated using the 2π multi-taper method (MTM) with a sliding time window (such as Fig. S1B). For the paleoclimate datasets spanning 0–800 ka, 800–1200 ka, and 1200–2700 ka, the sliding windows were set at 500 kyr, 200 kyr, and 500 kyr, respectively. (2) Then, the time-dependent amplitude modulations (power) at these three frequency bands were quantitatively calculated by integrating the evolutionary power at corresponding frequency bands. (3) Thereafter, to facilitate comparisons among different paleoclimate datasets, the integrated evolutionary spectral power at each specific band was normalized by the total evolutionary power (integrated from 0 to the Nyquist frequency) to get the evolution spectral power ratio. This is because the unit of different kind of paleoclimate proxies is different.

Over the last 2700 ka, the fundamental frequencies for precession and obliquity are 1/21 kyr-1 and 1/41 kyr-1. Thus, during the power integrating process, the frequency bands for the precession, obliquity, and ~100-kyr components were set to 1/18–1/26 kyr−1, 1/33.4–1/50.3 kyr-1, and 1/77–1/175 kyr-1, respectively.

Two software tools can be used to calculate the spectral power ratios: (1) the integratePower function in R package Astrochron, and (2) the Power Decomposition Analysis (PDA) function in Acycle software. The integratePower function processes both spectrograms (time-frequency or evolutionary spectra) and single spectra. Thus, for estimating the overall spectral power ratios of spectific frequenct bands in the clipped 0E0T-P series, we used integratePower function (e.g., Fig. 3J). Nevertheless, integratePower causes windows loss when estimating the evolutionary spectral power ratios, an issue resolved by the PDA function. Therefore, we used the PDA to calculate the evolutionary spectral power ratios for the 57 collected paleoclimate datasets.

Robustness estimation for the spectral power ratio results
Extracting evolutionary spectral power ratios is a non-stationary method and is relatively insensitive to age models because slight variations in the age model do not influence the long-term evolution trend of the spectral power ratio at a specific frequency. As a test, the evolution spectral power ratios at the precession and obliquity frequency bands for three different benthic δ18O stacks were examined (Fig. S1D, F, G). These stacks include the LR04 stack with LR04 age model, the LR04 stack with LR10 age model, and the Prob_stack, (Fig. S1D, F). The LR04 age model was established by tuning the δ18O stack to a target derived from an ice sheet model driven by 65°N summer insolation. The LR10 age model was based on the average sedimentation rate between tie points, independent of orbital forcing assumptions. The Prob_stack, compiled from 180 globally distributed benthic δ18O records and developed using a profile hidden Markov model, is more representative than the LR04 stack. Nevertheless, the Prob_stack adopted the LR04 age model as an initial condition during the stacking process, thereby inheriting the LR04 age model.

The calculated spectral power ratios of these stacks all show similar evolution trends, which also align with those acquired through the ENOF method (Fig. S1C, E). The ENOF is a non stationary method and employed to estimate the temporal amplitude of precession and obliquity in the benthic δ18O over the last 2700 ka. Therefore, the PDA method is also suitable for non-stationary analysis and can be regarded as an alternative to the ENOF method.

Heterogeneity in dataset length, age models, and orbital tuning may distort PDA results, potentially altering the spectral power ratio correlations. To mitigate these impacts, only PDA results from paleoclimate archives longer than 600 kyr over the past 800 ka were considered (Fig. S10C). Additionally, archives subjected to orbital tuning were separately assessed (Fig. S10D). To further reduce the effects of orbital tuning, datasets primarily constrained by the LR04 age model (Fig. S10E, F; Table S2) were tuned to the LR10 age model. The LR10 age model is independent of orbital tuning. Across all scenarios, the ~21-kyr power ratios negatively correlate with ~100-kyr power ratios, with no observed relationship between the ~41-kyr and ~100-kyr power ratios (Fig. S10). Additionally, the frequency bandwidth setting for the PDA does not influence the relationship among the ~21-kyr, ~41-kyr, and ~100-kyr power ratios (Fig. S11).

Phase coupling estimation between benthic δ13C and δ18O/ice volume
To obtain the phase relationship between benthic δ13C and δ18O/ice volume at the ~100-kyr timescale, the ~100-kyr components were initially extracted from benthic δ13C and δ18O/ice volume using a Gaussian bandpass filter with frequency bands setting of ~1/77–1/175 kyr-1. The Cross-Wavelet Transform (XWT), based on these filters was then estimated using the MATLAB Cross Wavelet and Wavelet Coherence Toolbox. To further quantitatively estimate their coupling relationship, The evolutionary correlation coefficient between the ~100-kyr filters of benthic δ13C and δ18O/ice volume was calculated with a 1000-kyr sliding windows. A correlation coefficient above 0.5 or below -0.5 indicates in-phase or antiphase coupling, respectively. To keep the consistency between δ18O and ice volume, the sea-level equivalents were reversed before these calculations.

Lead-lag relationship analysis
Lead-lag analysis was used to estimate the lead/lag relationship between two datasets, reference x and target y series. When target y lags behind reference x, then a positive lag value will be return, which means that reference x occurred earlier than y. The lead-lag relationship analysis was realized using Acycle software.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
This paper tackles a fundamental problem in understanding ice age behavior in the Pleistocene, which records several mysterious changes in behavior. No one doubts the critical influence of orbital cycles in controlling the timing of the ice age cycles, but no linear model comes close to capturing the geological observations. This paper attempts a statistical approach to the problem, using a variety of previously published archives of climate change.
Unfortunately, the paper is fundamentally flawed in its present form. I list below briefly major issues which I urge the authors to evaluate.
1. Although the role of CO2 is invoked frequently, high resolution and replicated estimates are only available for the past ~800,000 years. The record is being extended, most successfully in my opinion using the d11B proxy, but is incomplete. Critically, the proxy data do not support the idea of a gradual drawdown of CO2 at around the tijme of the MPT. Neither do temperature records show such a behavior. I do not see citations to these CO2 or SST reconstructions in the manuscript. Yet this argument of interglacial CO2 drawdown and cooling “pre-conditioning” ice sheet behavior during the subsequent glacial cycle is central to the interpretation here. The CO2 estimates used here consist of model results, using the d18O proxy and cannot be considered as independent of the isotopic data. They have not been validated with actual palo-CO2 estimates.
2. The authors assume that the isotope curve linearly reflects ice volume. Work over the last decade emphasizes the fact that there may be a significant, and evolving overprint of deep ocean temperature. Without separating temperature and ice volume, the interpretations presented here, which focus on the behavior of ice sheets, is incomplete and possibly incorrect. I’d urge them to look at the recent paper by Clark et al. in Science (2024) to see how much room for debate there is in interpreting what d18O is actually telling us.
3. The paper does not consider issues of age models and sampling resolution, both of which can be critical to isolating the precessional component in geological time series. Given “real-world” issues of sampling resolution and changes in sedimentation rate, accurately capturing precessional signals is quite difficult. A particular problem has to do with the potential circularity in assessing the phasing of precession relative to obliquity in records tuned to obliquity. As an example, the IODP 1385 age model referred to was “retuned” from the standard isotopic age model using a precessional signal by Liautaud et al. This retuning significantly increase the amplitude of the precessional signal, although it comes with its own assumptions.
4. The time series methods need to be better described. How do the authors treat non-stationarity? With moving windows? Given that precession is rarely resolved well in spectra of “real” data, how do they estimate uncertainties? And finally, how the “phase” is derived robustly is very difficult to determine, yet central to the conclusions.

Overall remarks
Zhang et al. provide new and compelling data analyses which show that the 100-kyr periodicity in Late Pleistocene climate archives likely derived from a change in the climate sensitivity to precession forcing prior to the Mid-Pleistocene transition (MPT). According to the authors, the link between precession and ice sheets is linked to the growth of ice sheets consecutively reaching the lower latitudes, where precession forcing becomes more and more influential on the glacial mass balance. This is a new and exciting discovery which will advance the field of both data and model paleo-science. I am convinced by the author’s data showing the change in sensitivity of climate to the precession forcing, and the subsequent hypothesis about gradual southward expansion of ice sheets against the backdrop of long-term CO2 decline. However, I currently disagree with the arguments in the last part of the manuscript which identify the onset of the MPT, and try to explain this mechanism to not just be a driver, but an instigator, of the MPT. In my opinion, shortening this section, and focusing on the manuscript’s main data analyses will elevate the manuscript and highlight the new findings that the analyses identify.
Additionally, the manuscript would benefit from including comparison of their findings and methods to other, already published, studies, such as work created by Huybers et al., or Berger et al. who either promote obliquity to control glacial-interglacial cycle development across the Pleistocene (both 41 and 100kyr worlds), or find precession to influence either the 41kyr or 100kyr-driven climate cycles. It would be very interesting to read the opinion of the authors on those findings, and how their own results fit into the already existing narratives. A final minor point, as I am not a specialist on the field of spectral analyses, but on data collection and MPT mechanisms, I sometimes found it difficult to follow the terminology in the current manuscript. I therefore included a list of suggestions below that hopefully help to clarify some questions and make the text more accessible to a wider audience. This includes minor changes, such as including definitions for certain spectral analysis vocabulary, and adding mathematical expressions of these definitions in the supplement, as well as adapting the figures for easier access.
Line by line comments
Main text:
Line 1: As I currently cannot support the final chapter of the manuscript (see comments below), I suggest to change the title to “CO2-forced change in glacial response to precession drives the Middle-Pleistocene Transition”
Line 38: are there any references that confirm the frequency of obliquity, precession, and eccentricity for a wider audience?
Line 52: Other references state that the 100kyr cycle is possibly not phase locked to eccentricity, but expresses multitides of precession and obliquity with internal feedback phase locking (e.g. Berger & Loutre, 2010, Global & Planetary change; Huybers & Wunsch, 2015, nature).
Line 63: It would be helpful to include definitions of the main concepts that will be used throughout the manuscript. These include spectral power, spectral phase, spectral power ratio, power shift. It would be supportive to have mathematical expressions of those definitions in the supplement as well.
Line 66: Briefly describe what the 57 paleoclimate archives are for a wider audience. I saw this information in the supplement, but briefly include why these 57 paleoclimate archives were chosen.
Line 82: The authors state in line 82 that the relationship between the 21kyr power ratio and the 100kyr power ratio holds during and before the MPT. However, the cross-plot in Figure 2 panel A has the highest r of 0.7. That surely shows that the relationship holds throughout?
Line 83: Can the authors comment on why their results show no link with obliquity, against what published studies have found (e.g. Feng & Bailer-Jones, 2015, QSR)
Line 94: can the authors confirm why the analysis was conducted on LR04, and not the 57 climate records which are plotted in Fig. 1?
Figure 3:
a) Can the authors include the mathematical expression in the supplement or reference the software, of how the derivative was calculated?
b) Also I suggest to change the y-axes labels to something more intuitive for wider audience accessibility, especially for panels C, D, E, F, K. I suggest the authors to consider a re-organisation of the panels. The small cross-plots (H, I, J) on the right invoke connection to panels E, F, G, which I believe is not the intention of the authors?
c) Considering B: can the authors comment on why this sea level record was chosen? There are other sea level records that could be used (e.g. Wang et al., 2010; de Boer et al., 2014, Sosdian et al. 2009, and others).
d) Have the authors considered looking at other CO2 records, such as Yamamoto et al., 2022? If so, why was the record in G chosen?
e) drawing the vertical dotted lines through the entire graph might be more intuitive for the reader
Line 186: I would be interested to see the author’s comment on the following publication here: Huybers et al., 2006, Science.
Line 200: It might be worth mentioning that ice sheets do not only drive internal variability, but can be affected by other internal feedback mechanisms themselves.
Figure 4. In general, I did not find this figure very intuitive and it took me some time to understand what the authors are trying to express. I kindly listed my issues and questions below.
a) Panel A: a wider audience will not be familiar with the term 1E1T-P. I assume this refers to the sum of all power spectra defined by the authors as Precession, Obliquity, Ecentricity. If so, I suggest to clarify this in the figure caption. I also suggest a small comment in the supplement, why this definition is chosen, and where it comes from. Maybe it is a common reference, but clarifying that would be useful.
b) Since the term power ratio is not necessarily well known to a wider audience, it would be useful to either have a clear definition in the text, or re-word the definition very brief in the figure or y-axis figure caption. Sometimes annotations may also help.
c) Is there a plot that shows the behaviour of obliquity in comparison to the plot in panel C? Also, for clarification, I assume that panel C is a cross-plot of panel B, is that correct?
d) Is the threshold in panel D just an example of a threshold, given that panel H and I show multiple thresholds on the x-axis?
e) I wonder whether it would be helpful to include a plot comparable to panel G, where each threshold’s power spectrum is plotted in the same plot, maybe using grey scales. Then the reader could see that changing the threshold will cause the appearance of the 95, 125, and 405 spectra.
f) The jump from panel D to panel F is counter-intuitive, since the y-axis are flipped on panel F. This needs to be clearly stated, or highlighted on the y-axis.
g) Using more descriptive titles on panels H, I, J would be useful.
h) The figure caption must include a description of what the whisker plots represent. I assume they represent the amplitude of the spectrum at each threshold? What are the error bars on the whisker plots?
i) In general, figure 4 is central to the hypothesis of the authors and shows the link between changes in climate sensitivity. Next to figure 2, it seems to be the most important figure. As such, I recommend the authors to consider re-organising the panels, or re-writing the figure caption, to help the general reader follow this information-heavy figure more easily.
Line 233: Can the authors comment on why they do not find any influence of obliquity on climate in comparison to other studies? (e.g. Huybers & Wunsch, 2015; Feng & Bailer-Jones, 2015; Berger et al., 2005, Paleoceanography). How do the author’s results compare to other studies finding precession to be a dominant driver (e.g. Liautaud et al., 2020, EPSL)?
Line 234: I was unable to follow the statement made in this sentence. Can the authors clarify why they claim that “the nonlinear amplification of 100kyr power is an intrinsic characteristic of the entire climate system, not just of ice volume?
Line 237: can the authors elaborate why multiple thresholds are needed to induce sensitivity change, and not just one threshold?
Line 240: I believe this analysis was conducted on data from LR04 correct? As such, why do the authors use LR04 as a proxy for global climate instead of ice volume, even though they have a perfect collection of 57 cores that are better at representing global climate than LR04?
Line 244: I cannot quite follow the argument in the following lines. Are the authors suggesting that the 100kyr cycle in LR04 occurs due to the 400kyr power in eccentricity, and therefore disagree with a collection of publications claiming that the 100kyr is a “quasi 100kyr” cycle modulated by precession and obliquity due to internal feedbacks? If so, this would be a new suggestion, and requires more in-depth discussion.
Line 262: At the moment, I cannot agree with this statement, since the authors receive different timings depending on whether their analysis uses LR04, or the probabilistic stack. Previously in the manuscript the authors argue that the use of the probabilistic stack is better, due to a more robust age model. I suggest that the authors stick with this logical approach, and present data from the probabilistic stack. The fact that all the other analyses show no sensitivity to different age models allows me to believe their results. In this case, I believe that the analysis shows sensitivity to age modelling, which in itself is an interesting result, but should not be over interpreted in terms of climate dynamics.
Line 259 and following section: In the following lines the authors present a hypothesis for how precession may drive the MPT. At this point, I am unable to agree with the hypothesis, due to (i) a lack of robust data which shows that the shift in sensitivity to the precession cycle, and re-location of power to 100kyr cycle is due to long-term reduction in pCO2 (see line 274). (ii) a mis-representation of reference 7 (see line 271). Reference 7 reviews processes that influence the MPT, but does not state significant hypotheses on how the MPT was instigated. In contrast, ref 7 proposes a collection of research questions which would be beneficial for the field to solve. (iii) a misrepresentation of refs 16, 45 (see line 278) which consider the late Pleistocene, not the early Pleistocene prior to the MPT. As such, their evidence needs to be used after large-scale ice sheets are already occurring (see line 281). (iv) the statement that “bedrock-mass-balance feedback and increased basal-sliding influences ice sheet dynamics” would benefit from more than ref 9, as this process has been suggested to influence ice sheets on multiple timescales, ie during deglaciations, or as an instigator for the MPT (see Regolith hypothesis, Clark et al., 2006). (v) a misrepresentation of ref 11 which only tested the change in long-term CO2 coupled to regolith removal, vs. only regolith removal. It did not test whether abrupt or gradual changes in CO2 cause the MPT.
Line 294: This statement is currently unsupported due to the above comments.
Line 297: Given that the probabilistic stack analyses of the authors show an onset at 1.2Ma, the literature seems to support the findings of the authors with respect to the probabilistic stack. Although I would suggest not putting too much influence on this analysis, as it seems highly variable to changes in age models, as the authors admit themselves in line 300.
Line 301: This sentence might need reworking.
Line 303: “High-amplitude” glacial cycles are generally believed to occur after 800kyr as they describe the 100kyr world glacial cycles, which occur after the MPT. Are the authors stating that they suggest an alternative idea?
Line 305: ref 47 needs to be discussed in line with more recent publications on this topic (some already listed throughout the review).
Line 308: At this point, I cannot agree with the conclusion that the MPT is a gradual process. The authors do not provide robust evidence for that, and the list of arguments is lacking. In fact, I am unsure whether the authors are able to supply this information with the data they have at this stage. I therefore suggest to shorten the last section, which should not take away from the novelty of the work presented before.
Figure 5:
a) The timing of 1452kyr seems dependent on the age model used which makes this graph hard to accept as robust
b) Improvement of the y-axis label would help with the understanding of the graph.
c) To help a wider audience, it might be useful to guide the reader through the cross plots and explain what the change in these patterns means for global climate. The correlations are compelling and I believe the analysis should focus more on the change in the correlation direction, which stays robust throughout different age models, rather than focusing on the timing of the MPT.
d) In the cross plot in panel D, E, the yellow line is annotated with p=0.86. Should this be r=0.86 or does it refer to a p-value? If so, maybe also report r.
Methods:
Line 439: Can this be expressed as a mathematical equation?
Line 442: It would be useful to include a detailed and clear definition for the different terms used throughout the manuscript, such as spectral power, spectral strength, spectral power ratio, spectral phase etc
Line 444: I wonder how different the age models are between these different approaches. Given the recent improvement in age modelling, the age models tested here might not vary greatly which could lead to internal age model errors per age model being larger than between- age model errors. Could the authors include a plot with one record on all age models so the variability can be compared? Alternatively, the authors could consider making a plot like S1 or S2, but using the maximum error values for one analysis and comparing to the minimum error values from the same age model from a second analysis. This should also show the influence of internal age model errors on the analyses.
Line 458: What do the authors mean by “robust” age models?
Line 476: Can this be expressed as a mathematical equation?

You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Earth’s climate has been dominated by ~100-kyr glacial cycles over the past ~800 ka, yet the mechanism remains debated. Here, we present correlation analyses of spectral power ratios of global records spanning the past 2.7 Ma, revealing a persistent anticorrelation between ~21-kyr and ~100-kyr power ratios, but no significant relationship between ~41-kyr and ~100-kyr power ratios. This suggests that ~100-kyr climate cycles are more related to eccentricity-modulated precession than to obliquity. Phase analyses of benthic δ18O/ice volume and δ13C (carbon cycle) since Antarctic glaciation onset (~34 Ma) show that strong ~100-kyr cycles emerged only when these proxies were phase-coupled. Such coupling recurred at ~2.4-Myr eccentricity maxima during the unipolar regime (before 7.5 Ma) and minima during the bipolar regime (after 4 Ma), explaining the persistent ~21-kyr/~100-kyr anticorrelation because eccentricity modulates precession amplitude. We propose that internal carbon cycle dynamics and ~2.4-Myr eccentricity-modulated δ¹⁸O/ice volume–δ¹³C coupling amplified ~100-kyr climate cycles not only over the past ~800 ka but since 34 Ma. Given that eccentricity will remain low for the next 400 kyr, ~100-kyr periodicities may continue to dominate future climate variability, assuming Earth remains in a bipolar regime.

---

## Introduction

As global cooling progressed through the Cenozoic, Arctic ice sheets began developing in the late Miocene, and large Northern Hemisphere ice sheets first emerged at the onset of the Pleistocene (~2.6-million-year age; Ma), marking Earth’s shift from a unipolar to a bipolar ice-sheet regime. Since then, Earth’s climate has been characterized by periodical glacial-interglacial cycles. The alignment of glacial cycles with astronomical periodicities leads to linking these climate cycles to variations in Earth’s orbital geometry and axial inclination that cause the insolation received on Earth to fluctuate at the frequency of obliquity (~1/41 kyr−1), precession (~1/19 and 1/23 kyr−1), and eccentricity (~1/100 and ~1/400 kyr−1). Obliquity alters the latitudinal distribution of insolation and seasonal contrast; precession affects the timing and intensity of seasons relative to Earth’s position in its elliptical orbit; and eccentricity influences the Earth–Sun distance, modulating the total insolation received by Earth. However, during the period after the Mid-Pleistocene Transition (MPT) (~800–1200 ka), the glacial-interglacial cycles display a dominant ~100-kyr cyclicities, no astronomical parameter could directly produce such strong ~100-kyr oscillations. This is because precession and obliquity cannot directly generate periodicities at ~100-kyr band, and eccentricity’s effect on total insolation is too weak to explain the strong ~100-kyr glacial power, despite eccentricity can produce ~100-kyr cycles. Amplitude mismatch between ~100 kyr cycles in eccentricity and climate, and the absence of the 405-kyr power in benthic foraminiferal oxygen isotope (δ18O), complicate the understanding of the ~100-kyr glacial cycles.

Before the MPT, glacial cycles were directly attributed to obliquity due to dominant ~40-kyr cyclicities, though interpretations for the dominance remain diverse. This idea was extended to explain the post-MPT ~100-kyr glacial cycles as a quantum of 2–3 obliquity cycles. Indeed, convincing evidence confirms obliquity’s role in late Pleistocene glacial terminations. However, the precession and obliquity phases of glacial terminations based on 230Th-dated speleothem chronology reveal that late Pleistocene glacial terminations have a closer relationship with precession than obliquity. This finding supports interpreting ~100-kyr cycles as a quantum of 4–6 precession cycles or a result of a beat between the main precessional frequencies. The research on the morphology of deglaciation/termination of glacial cycles further unveils that precession has more influence on deglacial onset, while obliquity is more important for attainment of peak interglacial conditions and glacial inception.

Despite these phase analyses confirm the role of astronomical forcing in driving glacial cycles, the mechanism behind dominant ~100-kyr power remains unclear. A comparison based on spectral analysis suggests that variations in inclination of Earth’s orbital plane could explain late Pleistocene ~100-kyr cycles. However, this is contested as an artifact of spectral methods, because unlike inclination’s singular ~100-kyr peak, glacial cycles exhibit variable ~80–120 kyr coeval periodicities.

In contrast to the external astronomical origin, late Pleistocene ~100-kyr glacial cycles were thought as the self-sustained oscillation driven by internal climate feedbacks. However, the solely internal mechanisms produce arbitrary phase, conflicting with the observed phase-locking between ~100-kyr cycles of eccentricity and climate. Thus, the plausible explanation for the late-Pleistocene ~100-kyr glacial cycle lies on the models that express these cycles as a nonlinear interaction between orbitally forced response (precession and obliquity) and the internal dynamics of atmosphere, oceans, ice sheets and lithosphere. This nonlinearity invokes a set of internal feedbacks to channel some of the system’s potential power into the ~100-kyr band. It is accepted that the ~100-kyr glacial cycles were phase-locked to eccentricity over the last 1.2 Ma, thus, the key to decoding the strong ~100-kyr glacial cycles depends on finding out the power source that amplifies the ~100-kyr spectral power. Both nonlinear response to precession and obliquity can produce ~100-kyr cycles, potentially amplifying ~100-kyr glacial power. Thus, confirming a potential link between the strong ~100-kyr glacial power and eccentricity-modulated precession or obliquity is pivotal to understanding glacial cycles. In this regard, analyzing the spectral power ratio relationship among the ~100-kyr cycles, precession, and obliquity components could provide clues.

The spectral power ratio relationship solely based on benthic δ18O lack statistical significance because the reverse relationship between the ~21-kyr and ~100-kyr power ratios in δ18O is masked by a nearly antiphase relationship between the ~41-kyr and ~100-kyr power ratio over the last 800 ka, which obscures the roles of precession and obliquity in amplifying ~100-kyr power. Nevertheless, as mentioned above, given that the ~100-kyr glacial cycles were closely related to internal processes, the 100-kyr cycles across climate components should be highly correlated with each other through a series of positive and negative feedbacks, despite potential time lags or leads between the forcing and the climate feedback. For example, the expansion and retreat of Pleistocene ice sheets could perturbate sea level and atmospheric-oceanic circulations via meltwater pulses and reshape Earth’s energy budget through albedo feedback. Consequently, the spectral power ratio relationship between precession/obliquity and the ~100-kyr components, preserved in ice volume or δ18O, should be projected onto other climate archives that are significantly affected by ice sheets. We therefore examine the spectral power ratio relationship among various paleoclimate proxies, including benthic δ18O, to explore the ~100-kyr glacial cycles. The spectral power ratio serves as a proxy for estimating spectral strength or variance within a specific frequency band (see Methods).

Given the shift from dominant ~40-kyr to ~100-kyr glacial cycles after the MPT and the current availability of high-resolution paleoclimate data, here, we statistically analyze spectral power ratio relationship among the ~21-kyr, ~41-kyr, and ~100-kyr components within datasets across 57 globally distributed paleoclimate archives (including ocean, loess, ice core, and other archives) from 33 sites. These continuous records span pre-MPT (1200–2700 ka), MPT (800–1200 ka), and post-MPT (0–800 ka) intervals, all with robust age models and a high temporal resolution of at least a 2-kyr sampling rate. The ~100-kyr power ratios display persistent negative correlation with ~21-kyr power ratios across these three intervals, while no relationship with ~41-kyr power ratios. Notably, strong/amplified ~100-kyr climate cycles also occurred before the Pleistocene, such as during the Pliocene, Miocene, and Oligocene. To test whether these earlier ~100-kyr climate cycles share a similar mechanism with those of the past 800 ka, we extend the analysis to the Eocene–Oligocene Transition (EOT; ~34 Ma), when the Antarctic ice sheet began to develop, by exploring the phase relationship between ice volume/benthic δ18O and benthic δ13C. It turns out that ~100-kyr climate cycles were periodically amplified, coinciding with δ18O/ice volume–δ13C phase coupling, which recurred at ~2.4-Myr eccentricity maxima (before 7.5 Ma) and minima (after 4 Ma).

---

## Results

The power decomposition analysis (PDA) (see Methods) was used to quantitatively estimate the spectral strength at frequencies corresponding to precession, obliquity, and ~100-kyr bands in paleoclimate records. Figure 2 presents the summarized PDA results for the collected 57 datasets, each based on their original age models, while detailed PDA results are shown in Figs. S2–S5. For comparisons, the overall power ratios of the ~100-kyr, ~41-kyr, and ~21-kyr cycles are shown using box whisker plots (Fig. 2A–C). To ensure significance, only PDA results with spectral power exceeding the 90% significance level at ~1/21 kyr−1, ~1/41 kyr−1, and ~1/100 kyr−1 were included. Detailed spectral estimations of these datasets are provided in Figs. S6–S9.

Post-MPT ~100-kyr power ratios exceed those of the pre-MPT interval in all datasets, while the opposite trend occurs for ~41-kyr power ratios. These shifts align with the transition from dominant ~41-kyr to ~100-kyr glacial cycles, confirming glacial influence on these records (Fig. 2A, C). Most paleoclimate records over the past ~800 ka show an inverse correlation between the ~100-kyr and ~21-kyr power ratios (Fig. 2A, B), a relationship that persists during and before the MPT (Fig. 2A, B). In contrast, the ~100-kyr power ratio shows no significant correlation with the ~41-kyr power ratio (Fig. 2A, C). Further analysis using the median power ratio values for the ~21-kyr, ~41-kyr, and ~100-kyr bands, represented by the horizontal lines in the box whisker plots, confirms a consistent negative correlation between the ~100-kyr and ~21-kyr power ratios (Fig. 2D, F, H), and no correlation between the ~100-kyr and ~41-kyr power ratios (Fig. 2E, G, I). Heterogeneity in dataset length, age models, and orbital tuning do not influence these relationship (Fig. S10C–F). Additionally, adjusting the frequency bandwidth setting in the PDA does not alter these relationships among the ~21-kyr, ~41-kyr, and ~100-kyr power ratios (Fig. S11).

---

## Methods

Extracting precession, obliquity and ~100-kyr spectral power ratios
To detect long-term evolution of changes in the spectral strength (or variance) of precession, obliquity, and ~100-kyr cycles in the collected climate archives, the evolutionary spectral power ratios at the precession, obliquity, and ~100-kyr bands to the total spectral power of the climate datasets were estimated. The estimation includes three steps. (1) Initially, the evolutionary power spectra of the datasets were calculated using the 2π multi-taper method (MTM) with a sliding time window (such as Fig. S1B). For the paleoclimate datasets spanning 0–800 ka, 800–1200 ka, and 1200–2700 ka, the sliding windows were set at 500 kyr, 200 kyr, and 500 kyr, respectively. (2) Then, the time-dependent amplitude modulations (power) at these three frequency bands were quantitatively calculated by integrating the evolutionary power at corresponding frequency bands. (3) Thereafter, to facilitate comparisons among different paleoclimate datasets, the integrated evolutionary spectral power at each specific band was normalized by the total evolutionary power (integrated from 0 to the Nyquist frequency) to get the evolution spectral power ratio. This is because the unit of different kind of paleoclimate proxies is different.

Over the last 2700 ka, the fundamental frequencies for precession and obliquity are 1/21 kyr-1 and 1/41 kyr-1. Thus, during the power integrating process, the frequency bands for the precession, obliquity, and ~100-kyr components were set to 1/18–1/26 kyr−1, 1/33.4–1/50.3 kyr-1, and 1/77–1/175 kyr-1, respectively.

Two software tools can be used to calculate the spectral power ratios: (1) the integratePower function in R package Astrochron, and (2) the Power Decomposition Analysis (PDA) function in Acycle software. The integratePower function processes both spectrograms (time-frequency or evolutionary spectra) and single spectra. Thus, for estimating the overall spectral power ratios of spectific frequenct bands in the clipped 0E0T-P series, we used integratePower function (e.g., Fig. 3J). Nevertheless, integratePower causes windows loss when estimating the evolutionary spectral power ratios, an issue resolved by the PDA function. Therefore, we used the PDA to calculate the evolutionary spectral power ratios for the 57 collected paleoclimate datasets.

Robustness estimation for the spectral power ratio results
Extracting evolutionary spectral power ratios is a non-stationary method and is relatively insensitive to age models because slight variations in the age model do not influence the long-term evolution trend of the spectral power ratio at a specific frequency. As a test, the evolution spectral power ratios at the precession and obliquity frequency bands for three different benthic δ18O stacks were examined (Fig. S1D, F, G). These stacks include the LR04 stack with LR04 age model, the LR04 stack with LR10 age model, and the Prob_stack, (Fig. S1D, F). The LR04 age model was established by tuning the δ18O stack to a target derived from an ice sheet model driven by 65°N summer insolation. The LR10 age model was based on the average sedimentation rate between tie points, independent of orbital forcing assumptions. The Prob_stack, compiled from 180 globally distributed benthic δ18O records and developed using a profile hidden Markov model, is more representative than the LR04 stack. Nevertheless, the Prob_stack adopted the LR04 age model as an initial condition during the stacking process, thereby inheriting the LR04 age model.

The calculated spectral power ratios of these stacks all show similar evolution trends, which also align with those acquired through the ENOF method (Fig. S1C, E). The ENOF is a non stationary method and employed to estimate the temporal amplitude of precession and obliquity in the benthic δ18O over the last 2700 ka. Therefore, the PDA method is also suitable for non-stationary analysis and can be regarded as an alternative to the ENOF method.

Heterogeneity in dataset length, age models, and orbital tuning may distort PDA results, potentially altering the spectral power ratio correlations. To mitigate these impacts, only PDA results from paleoclimate archives longer than 600 kyr over the past 800 ka were considered (Fig. S10C). Additionally, archives subjected to orbital tuning were separately assessed (Fig. S10D). To further reduce the effects of orbital tuning, datasets primarily constrained by the LR04 age model (Fig. S10E, F; Table S2) were tuned to the LR10 age model. The LR10 age model is independent of orbital tuning. Across all scenarios, the ~21-kyr power ratios negatively correlate with ~100-kyr power ratios, with no observed relationship between the ~41-kyr and ~100-kyr power ratios (Fig. S10). Additionally, the frequency bandwidth setting for the PDA does not influence the relationship among the ~21-kyr, ~41-kyr, and ~100-kyr power ratios (Fig. S11).

Phase coupling estimation between benthic δ13C and δ18O/ice volume
To obtain the phase relationship between benthic δ13C and δ18O/ice volume at the ~100-kyr timescale, the ~100-kyr components were initially extracted from benthic δ13C and δ18O/ice volume using a Gaussian bandpass filter with frequency bands setting of ~1/77–1/175 kyr-1. The Cross-Wavelet Transform (XWT), based on these filters was then estimated using the MATLAB Cross Wavelet and Wavelet Coherence Toolbox. To further quantitatively estimate their coupling relationship, The evolutionary correlation coefficient between the ~100-kyr filters of benthic δ13C and δ18O/ice volume was calculated with a 1000-kyr sliding windows. A correlation coefficient above 0.5 or below -0.5 indicates in-phase or antiphase coupling, respectively. To keep the consistency between δ18O and ice volume, the sea-level equivalents were reversed before these calculations.

Lead-lag relationship analysis
Lead-lag analysis was used to estimate the lead/lag relationship between two datasets, reference x and target y series. When target y lags behind reference x, then a positive lag value will be return, which means that reference x occurred earlier than y. The lead-lag relationship analysis was realized using Acycle software.

No one doubts the critical influence of orbital cycles in controlling the timing of the ice age cycles, but no linear model comes close to capturing the geological observations. 144 Our reply: In terms of the time series methods, we used the power decomposition
145 analysis (PDA) (Li et al., 2019). This method allows for the quantitative estimation of
146 the influence of precession, obliquity, and ~100-kyr cycles on paleoclimate archives.
147 Analogous to the Empirical Nonlinear Orbital Fitting (ENOF) method (Liautaud et al.,
148 2020), this non-stationary technique, PDA, employs a sliding time window to calculate
149 evolutionary power ratios within specific frequency bands (Fig. S1). For the
150 paleoclimate datasets spanning 0–800 ka, 800–1200 ka, and 1200–2700 ka, the sliding
151 windows were set at 500 kyr, 200 kyr, and 500 kyr, respectively.
152 In the revised manuscript, we have added more details to introduce the PDA
153 method (see Method section) and rewrote the first section of the Method to improve
154 clarity on the principles and processing steps of PDA. The revised description is as
155 follows: (1) Initially, the evolutionary power spectra of the datasets were calculated
156 using the 2π multi-taper method (MTM) (Thomson, 1982) with a sliding time window
157 (Meyers et al., 2012) (Fig. S1B). (2) Next, the time-dependent amplitude modulations
158 (power) at these three frequency bands (~1/21 kyr-1, ~1/41 kyr-1, and ~1/100 kyr-1) were
159 quantitatively calculated by integrating the evolutionary power at the corresponding
160 frequency bands (Meyers et al., 2012; Li et al., 2019). (3) Thereafter, to facilitate
161 comparisons among different paleoclimate datasets, the integrated evolutionary spectral
162 power at each specific band was normalized by the total evolutionary power (integrated
163 from 0 to the Nyquist frequency) to obtain the evolution spectral power ratio. This
164 process is necessary because different paleoclimate proxies have varying units.
165 Moreover, to better illustrate this method, the evolution spectral power ratios at the
166 precession and obliquity frequency bands for three different benthic δ18O stacks were
167 examined. These include the LR04 stack (Lisiecki and Raymo, 2005), the Prob_stack
168 (Ahn et al., 2017), and the H07&NA stack (Huybers, 2007) (Fig. S1D, F). The
169 calculated spectral power ratios from these stack exhibit similar evolution trends,
170 consistent with the results obtained through the Empirical Nonlinear Orbital Fitting
171 (ENOF) (Fig. S1C, E) (Liautaud et al., 2020).

### Reviewer 3

Overall remarks
Zhang et al. provide new and compelling data analyses which show that the 100-kyr periodicity in Late Pleistocene climate archives likely derived from a change in the climate sensitivity to precession forcing prior to the Mid-Pleistocene transition (MPT). According to the authors, the link between precession and ice sheets is linked to the growth of ice sheets consecutively reaching the lower latitudes, where precession forcing becomes more and more influential on the glacial mass balance. This is a new and exciting discovery which will advance the field of both data and model paleo-science. I am convinced by the author’s data showing the change in sensitivity of climate to the precession forcing, and the subsequent hypothesis about gradual southward expansion of ice sheets against the backdrop of long-term CO2 decline. However, I currently disagree with the arguments in the last part of the manuscript which identify the onset of the MPT, and try to explain this mechanism to not just be a driver, but an instigator, of the MPT. In my opinion, shortening this section, and focusing on the manuscript’s main data analyses will elevate the manuscript and highlight the new findings that the analyses identify.
Additionally, the manuscript would benefit from including comparison of their findings and methods to other, already published, studies, such as work created by Huybers et al., or Berger et al. who either promote obliquity to control glacial-interglacial cycle development across the Pleistocene (both 41 and 100kyr worlds), or find precession to influence either the 41kyr or 100kyr-driven climate cycles. It would be very interesting to read the opinion of the authors on those findings, and how their own results fit into the already existing narratives. A final minor point, as I am not a specialist on the field of spectral analyses, but on data collection and MPT mechanisms, I sometimes found it difficult to follow the terminology in the current manuscript. I therefore included a list of suggestions below that hopefully help to clarify some questions and make the text more accessible to a wider audience. This includes minor changes, such as including definitions for certain spectral analysis vocabulary, and adding mathematical expressions of these definitions in the supplement, as well as adapting the figures for easier access.
